claims.text: Doping the HEA layer with a high-thermal-conductivity secondary phase will create a controlled thermal-conductivity gradient across the layer.
The controlled thermal-conductivity gradient will improve heat-transfer capability.
The intervention will preserve structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
Ceramic particles or metallic inclusions can serve as a secondary phase having significantly higher thermal conductivity than the HEA.
The proposed behavior should hold over 300–1500°C.
The proposed behavior should hold under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses typical of plasma-facing reactor environments.
The intervention will produce a controlled dispersion of the secondary phase within the HEA matrix.
The dispersed secondary phase will create localized heat-conduction pathways.
Localized heat-conduction pathways will enhance the overall thermal conductivity of the HEA layer.
The HEA matrix's high entropy provides resistance to phase separation.
Resistance to phase separation will allow the doped HEA to retain structural integrity.
The doped HEA will have higher heat-transfer capability than an undoped HEA layer under similar conditions.
The doped HEA will show no significant degradation in mechanical properties relative to the undoped HEA under the specified conditions.
Excessive brittleness or phase instability caused by the secondary phase could prevent the hypothesis from holding.
Thermal-conductivity improvement depends on the identity and dispersion of the secondary phase.
Mechanical-property preservation depends on the identity and dispersion of the secondary phase.
